instagram_caption:
🚀 Private credit went from “nobody’s business” to a $1.7T heavyweight—while traditional lending stalled.

Here’s the timeline comparison that explains why investors kept moving off public markets and into private deals. In 2009, private credit was about $80B. By 2014 it had crossed ~$200B—still small, but clearly no longer a niche. The post-crisis world had a problem: banks were tightening credit, regulators were pushing balance-sheet caution, and borrowers still needed funding.

Then the pace turned dramatic. From 2015 to 2018, private credit climbed from ~$310B to ~$610B as deal execution became faster and underwriting stayed largely private (no daily tape pressure, no secondary-market volatility forcing repricing). At the same time, US banks didn’t “shrink”—but their C&I lending trend flattened and eventually started slipping relative to the alternative channel. Bank C&I loans moved up early (about $2150B in 2009 to ~$2950B by 2019), but the momentum softened right as private credit took off.

The turning point wasn’t just growth—it was a shock. In 2020, when public credit markets seized, leveraged lending and high-yield still had liquidity, but the market confidence gap widened. Private credit jumped from ~$760B (2019) to about ~$980B (2020). The 2021 inflow wave was even louder: ~$980B → ~$1180B. Meanwhile public benchmarks kept swelling too—leveraged loans rose from ~$1800B (2020) to ~$2200B (2021)—but private credit carved out a distinct lane: borrower-by-borrower structures, yield targets, and long-dated commitments.

Now watch the contrast: 2022 rate shock rattled everything. Leveraged loans slipped (~$2200B → ~$1900B) and high-yield dipped (~$1700B → ~$1550B). Private credit still climbed (~$1180B → ~$1360B). By 2024 it’s around ~$1540B, and the 2026 projection/estimate hits ~$1700B.

If private credit is the “shadow banking” story—what do you think happens next: does it keep absorbing more lending share, or does regulation/competition cap the growth curve?

facebook_caption:
Private credit has transformed from a niche strategy into a large, fast-growing segment of the lending economy. In 2009, private credit assets were roughly $80B. Over the next decade they rose steadily—crossing ~$200B by 2014 and accelerating through 2015–2018 from about ~$310B to ~$610B.

The inflection point came during the 2020 shock. While public credit markets and risk appetite were disrupted, private underwriting structures continued to attract allocations. Private credit rose from about ~$760B in 2019 to ~$980B in 2020, then accelerated further in 2021 to about ~$1180B.

The chart also highlights the “traditional channel” pressure. US bank C&I loans increased up to the late-2010s (about $2150B in 2009 to ~$2950B by 2019) but then softened amid tightening and repricing pressures, moving toward ~$2700B by 2024.

Public market benchmarks show the volatility backdrop: leveraged loans grew strongly into 2021 (around $1800B → ~$2200B) before easing in 2022 (~$1900B), and high-yield bonds also fell in 2022 (~$1700B → ~$1550B). Yet private credit continued trending upward through that period (about ~$1180B → ~$1360B).

By 2026, the private credit line reaches an estimated ~$1700B—illustrating how private markets have increasingly competed with (and complemented) banks and public credit.
